Main.sentence: The North Atlantic Treaty Organization ( NATO /ˈneɪtoʊ/ ___E:NAY-toh U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key)___ ; ___E:French U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language)___ : Organisation du traité de l'Atlantique Nord , OTAN ), also called the North Atlantic Alliance , is an ___E:intergovernmental U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intergovernmental_organization)___ ___E:military alliance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_alliance)___ between ___E:32 member states U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_states_of_NATO)___ —30 in ___E:Europe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe)___ and 2 in ___E:North America U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America)___ .

Founded in the ___E:aftermath of World War II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aftermath_of_World_War_II)___ , NATO was established with the signing of the ___E:North Atlantic Treaty U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Atlantic_Treaty)___ in 1949. The organization serves as a system of ___E:collective security U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collective_security)___ , whereby its independent member states agree to mutual defence in response to an attack by any outside party.
This is enshrined in Article 5 of the treaty, which states that an armed attack against one member shall be considered an attack against them all.

Throughout the ___E:Cold War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War)___ , NATO's primary purpose was to deter and counter the threat posed by the ___E:Soviet Union U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union)___ and its ___E:satellite states U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satellite_state)___ , which formed the rival ___E:Warsaw Pact U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw_Pact)___ in 1955. Following the ___E:dissolution of the Soviet Union U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dissolution_of_the_Soviet_Union)___ in 1991, the alliance adapted, conducting its first major military interventions ___E:in Bosnia and Herzegovina U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO_intervention_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina)___ (1992–1995) and ___E:Yugoslavia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO_bombing_of_Yugoslavia)___ (1999).

Article 5 was invoked for the first and only time after the ___E:September 11 attacks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11_attacks)___ , leading to the deployment of NATO troops to ___E:Afghanistan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghanistan)___ as part of the ___E:International Security Assistance Force U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Security_Assistance_Force)___ (ISAF).

The alliance has since been involved in a range of roles, including ___E:training in Iraq U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO_Training_Mission_%E2%80%93_Iraq)___ , ___E:intervention in Libya U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_military_intervention_in_Libya)___ in 2011, and ___E:countering piracy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Ocean_Shield)___ .

Since the end of the Cold War, the alliance has ___E:accepted sixteen new members U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enlargement_of_NATO)___ , incorporating former ___E:Warsaw Pact U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw_Pact)___ countries and ___E:post-Soviet states U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-Soviet_states)___ .

NATO and Russia ___E:have co-operated U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia%E2%80%93NATO_relations)___ , but Russian leaders have called this eastward enlargement a threat to its security interests, and ___E:oppose Ukraine joining U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_opposition_to_Ukrainian_NATO_membership)___ NATO. The ___E:Russian annexation of Crimea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_annexation_of_Crimea)___ in 2014 prompted strong condemnation from NATO and a renewed focus on collective defence.

Russia's ___E:full-scale invasion of Ukraine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine)___ in 2022 led to a major reinforcement of NATO's eastern flank and caused ___E:Finland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finland)___ and ___E:Sweden U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweden)___ to abandon their neutral status and join the alliance.

NATO recognizes ___E:Bosnia and Herzegovina U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosnia_and_Herzegovina)___ , ___E:Ukraine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukraine)___ and ___E:Georgia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(country))___ as aspiring members.

___E:NATO's main headquarters U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO_headquarters)___ are in ___E:Brussels U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brussels)___ , Belgium, while ___E:its military headquarters U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Headquarters_Allied_Powers_Europe)___ are near ___E:Mons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mons,_Belgium)___ , Belgium.
The combined militaries of all NATO members include approximately 3.5 million soldiers and personnel.
Their combined military spending constitutes over half of the ___E:global total U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_with_highest_military_expenditures)___ .

Members have committed to a target of spending at least 5% of their ___E:gross domestic product U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gross_domestic_product)___ (GDP) on defence to ensure the alliance's continued military readiness.
NATO has its roots in the ___E:Atlantic Charter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Charter)___ , a 1941 agreement between the United States and United Kingdom.
The Charter laid out a framework for international cooperation without territorial expansion after ___E:World War II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II)___ .

On 4 March 1947, the ___E:Treaty of Dunkirk U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Dunkirk)___ was signed by France and the United Kingdom during the ___E:aftermath of World War II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aftermath_of_World_War_II)___ and the ___E:start of the Cold War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War_(1947%E2%80%931953))___ as a Treaty of Alliance and Mutual Assistance in the event of possible attacks by Germany.

In March 1948, this alliance was expanded in the ___E:Treaty of Brussels U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Brussels)___ to include the ___E:Benelux U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benelux)___ countries, forming the Brussels Treaty Organization, commonly known as the ___E:Western Union U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Union_(alliance))___ .

Talks for a wider military alliance, which could include North America, also began that month in the United States, where their foreign policy under the ___E:Truman Doctrine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truman_Doctrine)___ set out in 1947 promoted international solidarity against actions they saw as communist aggression, such as the ___E:February 1948 coup d'état in Czechoslovakia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1948_Czechoslovak_coup_d%27%C3%A9tat)___ .

These talks resulted in the signature of the ___E:North Atlantic Treaty U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Atlantic_Treaty)___ on 4 April 1949 by the member states of the Western Union plus the United States, Canada, Portugal, Italy, Norway, Denmark, and Iceland.
Canadian diplomat ___E:Lester B. Pearson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lester_B._Pearson)___ was a key author and drafter of the treaty.

The North Atlantic Treaty was largely dormant until the ___E:Korean War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_War)___ initiated the establishment of NATO to implement it with an integrated military structure.

This included the formation of ___E:Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Headquarters_Allied_Powers_Europe)___ (SHAPE) in 1951, which adopted many of the Western Union's military structures and plans,  including their ___E:agreements on standardizing equipment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standardization_Agreement)___ and ___E:agreements on stationing foreign military forces U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Status_of_forces_agreement)___ in European countries.
In 1952, the post of ___E:Secretary General of NATO U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_General_of_NATO)___ was established as the organization's chief civilian.

That year also saw the first major NATO ___E:maritime exercises U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_exercise)___ , ___E:Exercise Mainbrace U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exercise_Mainbrace)___ and the accession of ___E:Greece U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greece)___ and ___E:Turkey U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey)___ to the organization.

Following the ___E:London and Paris Conferences U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_and_Paris_Conferences)___ , ___E:West Germany U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Germany)___ was permitted to rearm militarily, as they joined NATO in May 1955, which was, in turn, a major factor in the creation of the Soviet-dominated ___E:Warsaw Pact U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw_Pact)___ , delineating the two opposing sides of the ___E:Cold War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War)___ .
The building of the ___E:Berlin Wall U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Wall)___ in 1961 marked a height in Cold War tensions, when 400,000 US troops were stationed in Europe.

Doubts over the strength of the relationship between the European states and the United States ebbed and flowed, along with doubts over the credibility of the NATO defence against a prospective Soviet invasion – doubts that led to the development of the ___E:independent French nuclear deterrent U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strike_Force_(France))___ and the withdrawal of ___E:France U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France)___ from NATO's military structure in 1966.   In 1982, the newly democratic Spain joined the alliance.
The ___E:Revolutions of 1989 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolutions_of_1989)___ in Europe led to a strategic re-evaluation of NATO's purpose, nature, tasks, and focus on the continent.

In October 1990, ___E:East Germany U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Germany)___ ___E:became part of the Federal Republic of Germany U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_reunification)___ and the alliance, and in November 1990, the alliance signed the ___E:Treaty on Conventional Armed Forces in Europe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_on_Conventional_Armed_Forces_in_Europe)___ (CFE) in Paris with the Soviet Union.

It mandated specific military reductions across the continent, which continued after the collapse of the ___E:Warsaw Pact U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw_Pact)___ in February 1991 and the ___E:dissolution of the Soviet Union U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dissolution_of_the_Soviet_Union)___ that December, which removed the de facto main adversaries of NATO.  This began a drawdown of military spending and equipment in Europe.

The CFE treaty allowed signatories to remove 52,000 pieces of conventional armaments in the following sixteen years,  and allowed military spending by NATO's European members to decline by 28 percent from 1990 to 2015.  In 1990, several Western leaders gave assurances to ___E:Mikhail Gorbachev U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikhail_Gorbachev)___ that NATO would not expand further east, as revealed by memoranda of private conversations.
In the 1990s, the organization extended its activities into political and humanitarian situations that had not formerly been NATO concerns.

During the ___E:breakup of Yugoslavia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breakup_of_Yugoslavia)___ , the organization conducted its first ___E:military interventions U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_NATO_operations)___ in ___E:Bosnia from 1992 to 1995 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO_intervention_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina)___ and later ___E:Yugoslavia in 1999 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_NATO_bombing_of_Yugoslavia)___ .

Politically, the organization sought better relations with the newly autonomous ___E:Central and Eastern European U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_and_Eastern_Europe)___ states, and diplomatic forums for regional cooperation between NATO and its neighbours were set up during this post-Cold War period, including the ___E:Partnership for Peace U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partnership_for_Peace)___ and the ___E:Mediterranean Dialogue U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean_Dialogue)___ initiative in 1994, the ___E:Euro-Atlantic Partnership Council U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euro-Atlantic_Partnership_Council)___ in 1997, and the ___E:NATO–Russia Permanent Joint Council U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO%E2%80%93Russia_relations)___ in 1998. At the ___E:1999 Washington summit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_Washington_summit)___ , ___E:Hungary U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary)___ , ___E:Poland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poland)___ , and the ___E:Czech Republic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czech_Republic)___ officially joined NATO, and the organization also issued new guidelines for membership with individualized " ___E:Membership Action Plans U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Membership_Action_Plan)___ ".
These plans governed the subsequent addition of new alliance members.

___E:Article 5 of the North Atlantic treaty U:(https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/North_Atlantic_Treaty#Article_5)___ , requiring member states to come to the aid of any member state subject to an armed attack, was invoked for the first and only time after the ___E:September 11 attacks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11_attacks)___ ,  after which troops were deployed to ___E:Afghanistan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghanistan)___ under the NATO-led ___E:ISAF U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Security_Assistance_Force)___ .

The organization has operated a range of additional roles since then, including sending ___E:trainers to Iraq U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO_Training_Mission_%E2%80%93_Iraq)___ , assisting in ___E:counter-piracy operations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Ocean_Shield)___ .

The election of French president ___E:Nicolas Sarkozy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolas_Sarkozy)___ in 2007 led to a major reform of France's military position, culminating with the return to full membership on 4 April 2009, which also included France rejoining the ___E:NATO Military Command Structure U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO_Military_Command_Structure)___ , while maintaining an independent nuclear deterrent.

The 2014 ___E:Russian annexation of Crimea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annexation_of_Crimea_by_the_Russian_Federation)___ led to strong condemnation by all NATO members,  and was one of the seven times that ___E:Article 4 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Atlantic_Treaty#Article_4)___ , which calls for consultation among NATO members, has been invoked.
Prior times included during the ___E:Iraq War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_War)___ and ___E:Syrian civil war U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syrian_civil_war)___ .

At the ___E:2014 Wales summit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Wales_summit)___ , the leaders of NATO's member states formally committed for the first time to spend the equivalent of at least two percent of their ___E:gross domestic products U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gross_domestic_product)___ on defence by 2024, which had previously been only an informal guideline.

At the ___E:2016 Warsaw summit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Warsaw_summit)___ , NATO countries agreed on the creation of ___E:NATO Enhanced Forward Presence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO_Enhanced_Forward_Presence)___ , which deployed four multinational battalion-sized battlegroups in Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, and Poland.

Before and during the ___E:2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine)___ , several NATO countries sent ground troops, warships and fighter aircraft to reinforce the alliance's eastern flank, and multiple countries again invoked Article 4.    In March 2022, NATO leaders met at Brussels for an ___E:extraordinary summit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Brussels_summit)___ which also involved ___E:Group of Seven U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_of_Seven)___ and European Union leaders.

NATO member states agreed to establish four additional battlegroups in Bulgaria, Hungary, Romania, and Slovakia,  and elements of the ___E:NATO Response Force U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO_Response_Force)___ were activated for the first time in NATO's history.
As of June 2022, NATO had deployed 40,000 troops along its 2,500-kilometre-long (1,550 mi) Eastern flank to deter Russian aggression.
More than half of this number have been deployed in Bulgaria, Romania, Hungary, Slovakia, and Poland, which five countries muster a considerable combined ex-NATO force of 259,000 troops.

To supplement Bulgaria's Air Force, Spain sent ___E:Eurofighter Typhoons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurofighter_Typhoon)___ , the Netherlands sent eight ___E:F-35 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_Martin_F-35_Lightning_II)___ attack aircraft, and additional French and US attack aircraft would arrive soon as well.  In 2025, Germany stationed a full armoured brigade in Lithuania.

No military operations were conducted by NATO during the Cold War. Following the end of the Cold War, the first operations, Anchor Guard in 1990 and Ace Guard in 1991, were prompted by the ___E:Iraqi invasion of Kuwait U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraqi_invasion_of_Kuwait)___ .
Airborne early warning aircraft were sent to provide coverage of southeastern Turkey, and later a quick-reaction force was deployed to the area.
The ___E:Bosnian War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosnian_War)___ began in 1992, as a result of the ___E:breakup of Yugoslavia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breakup_of_Yugoslavia)___ .

The deteriorating situation led to ___E:United Nations Security Council Resolution 816 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council_Resolution_816)___ on 9 October 1992, authorizing its member-states to enforce a previously declared ___E:no-fly zone U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No-fly_zone)___ under the ___E:United Nations Protection Force U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Protection_Force)___ over central Bosnia and Herzegovina.
NATO complied and started enforcing the ban on 12 April 1993 with ___E:Operation Deny Flight U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Deny_Flight)___ .

From June 1993 until October 1996, ___E:Operation Sharp Guard U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Sharp_Guard)___ added maritime enforcement of the ___E:arms embargo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arms_embargo)___ and ___E:economic sanctions U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_sanctions)___ against the ___E:Federal Republic of Yugoslavia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Republic_of_Yugoslavia)___ .
On 28 February 1994, NATO took its first wartime action by ___E:shooting down four Bosnian Serb aircraft U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banja_Luka_incident)___ violating the no-fly zone.

On 10 and 11 April 1994, the United Nations Protection Force called in air strikes to protect the ___E:Goražde U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gora%C5%BEde)___ safe area, resulting in the bombing of a Bosnian Serb military command outpost near Goražde by two US ___E:F-16 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Dynamics_F-16_Fighting_Falcon)___ jets acting under NATO direction.
In retaliation, Serbs took 150 U.N. personnel hostage on 14 April.
On 16 April a British ___E:Sea Harrier U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Aerospace_Sea_Harrier)___ was shot down over Goražde by Serb forces.

In August 1995, a two-week NATO bombing campaign, ___E:Operation Deliberate Force U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_NATO_bombing_campaign_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina)___ , began against the ___E:Army of the Republika Srpska U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Army_of_the_Republika_Srpska)___ , after the ___E:Srebrenica genocide U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Srebrenica_massacre)___ .

Further NATO air strikes helped bring the ___E:Yugoslav Wars U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yugoslav_Wars)___ to an end, resulting in the ___E:Dayton Agreement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dayton_Agreement)___ in November 1995.  As part of this agreement, NATO deployed a UN-mandated peacekeeping force, under ___E:Operation Joint Endeavor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Joint_Endeavor)___ , named ___E:IFOR U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IFOR)___ .
Almost 60,000 NATO troops were joined by forces from non-NATO countries in this peacekeeping mission.

This transitioned into the smaller ___E:SFOR U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SFOR)___ , which started with 32,000 troops initially and ran from December 1996 until December 2004, when operations were then passed onto the ___E:European Union Force Althea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Althea)___ .
Following the lead of its member states, NATO began to award a service medal, the ___E:NATO Medal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO_Medal)___ , for these operations.

In an effort to stop ___E:Slobodan Milošević U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slobodan_Milo%C5%A1evi%C4%87)___ 's Serbian-led crackdown on ___E:KLA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kosovo_Liberation_Army)___ separatists and Albanian civilians in ___E:Kosovo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kosovo)___ , the ___E:United Nations Security Council U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council)___ passed ___E:Resolution 1199 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council_Resolution_1199)___ on 23 September 1998 to demand a ceasefire.

Negotiations under US Special Envoy ___E:Richard Holbrooke U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Holbrooke)___ broke down on 23 March 1999, and he handed the matter to NATO,  which acted on protecting regional security and started a 78-day bombing campaign on 24 March 1999.  Operation Allied Force targeted the military capabilities of what was then the ___E:Federal Republic of Yugoslavia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Republic_of_Yugoslavia)___ .

During the crisis, NATO also deployed one of its international reaction forces, the ___E:ACE Mobile Force (Land) U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACE_Mobile_Force_(Land))___ , to Albania as the Albania Force (AFOR), to deliver humanitarian aid to refugees from Kosovo.

The campaign was and has been criticized over ___E:its civilian casualties U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civilian_casualties_during_Operation_Allied_Force)___ , including the bombing of the ___E:Chinese embassy in Belgrade U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._bombing_of_the_Chinese_embassy_in_Belgrade)___ , and over ___E:whether it had legitimacy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legitimacy_of_the_NATO_bombing_of_Yugoslavia)___ .

The US, the UK, and most other NATO countries opposed efforts to require the UN Security Council to approve NATO military strikes, such as the action against Serbia in 1999, while France and some others [specify] claimed that the alliance needed UN approval.

The US/UK side claimed that this would undermine the authority of the alliance, and they noted that Russia and China would have exercised their Security Council vetoes to block the strike on ___E:Yugoslavia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yugoslavia)___ , and could do the same in future conflicts where NATO intervention was required, thus nullifying the entire potency and purpose of the organization.

Recognizing the post-Cold War military environment, NATO adopted the Alliance Strategic Concept during its ___E:Washington summit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_Washington_summit)___ in April 1999 that emphasized conflict prevention and crisis management.
Milošević finally accepted the terms of an international peace plan on 3 June 1999, ending the ___E:Kosovo War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kosovo_War)___ .

On 11 June, Milošević further accepted ___E:UN resolution 1244 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council_Resolution_1244)___ , under the mandate of which NATO then helped establish the ___E:KFOR U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kosovo_Force)___ peacekeeping force.
Nearly one million refugees had fled Kosovo, and part of KFOR's mandate was to protect the humanitarian missions, in addition to deterring violence.

In August–September 2001, the alliance also mounted ___E:Operation Essential Harvest U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Essential_Harvest)___ , a mission disarming ethnic Albanian militias in the Republic of Macedonia.
As of 2023 [update] , around 4,500 KFOR soldiers, representing 27 countries, continue to operate in the area.

The ___E:September 11 attacks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11_attacks)___ in the United States caused NATO to invoke ___E:Article 5 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO_Article_5)___ of the NATO Charter for the first time in the organization's history.

The Article states that an attack on any member shall be considered to be an attack on all. The invocation was confirmed on 4 October 2001 when NATO determined that the attacks were indeed eligible under the terms of the North Atlantic Treaty.

The eight official actions taken by NATO in response to the attacks included ___E:Operation Eagle Assist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Eagle_Assist)___ and ___E:Operation Active Endeavour U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Active_Endeavour)___ , a naval operation in the Mediterranean Sea designed to prevent the movement of terrorists or weapons of mass destruction, and to enhance the security of shipping in general, which began on 4 October 2001.

Turkey invoked the first Article 4 meetings in 2003 at the start of the ___E:Iraq War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_War)___ .

The 32 NATO members are:
NATO has thirty-two members, mostly in Europe with two in North America.

NATO's "area of responsibility", within which attacks on member states are eligible for an Article 5 response, is defined under Article 6 of the ___E:North Atlantic Treaty U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Atlantic_Treaty)___ to include member territory in Europe, North America, Turkey, and islands in the North Atlantic north of the ___E:Tropic of Cancer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropic_of_Cancer)___ .
Attacks on vessels, aircraft and other forces in the North Atlantic (again, north of the Tropic of Cancer) and the Mediterranean Sea may also provoke an Article 5 response.

During the original treaty negotiations, the United States insisted that colonies such as the ___E:Belgian Congo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgian_Congo)___ be excluded from the treaty.   ___E:French Algeria U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Algeria)___ was, however, covered until ___E:its independence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1962_Algerian_independence_referendum)___ on 3 July 1962.  Twelve of these thirty-two are original members who joined in 1949, while the other twenty joined in one of ten enlargement rounds.

The three Nordic countries which joined NATO as founding members, Denmark, Iceland, and Norway, chose to limit their participation in three areas: there would be no permanent peacetime bases, no nuclear warheads and no Allied military activity (unless invited) permitted on their territory.

However, Denmark allows the ___E:U.S. Space Force U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Space_Force)___ to maintain ___E:Pituffik Space Base U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pituffik_Space_Base)___ , in Greenland.

From the mid-1960s to the mid-1990s, France pursued a military strategy of independence from NATO under a policy dubbed "Gaullo-Mitterrandism".  ___E:Nicolas Sarkozy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolas_Sarkozy)___ negotiated the return of France to the integrated military command and the Defence Planning Committee in 2009, the latter being disbanded the following year. France remains the only NATO member outside the Nuclear Planning Group and, unlike the United States and the United Kingdom, will not commit its nuclear-armed submarines to the alliance.
NATO was established on 4 April 1949 by the signing of the ___E:North Atlantic Treaty U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Atlantic_Treaty)___ (Washington Treaty).
The 12 founding members of the alliance were Belgium, Canada, Denmark, France, Iceland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, the United Kingdom, and the United States.
Four new members joined during the Cold War: Greece (1952), Turkey (1952), ___E:West Germany U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Germany)___ (1955) and Spain (1982).

Following the ___E:dissolution of the Soviet Union U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dissolution_of_the_Soviet_Union)___ , many former ___E:Warsaw Pact U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw_Pact)___ and ___E:post-Soviet states U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-Soviet_states)___ sought membership.

In 1990, the territory of the former ___E:East Germany U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Germany)___ was added with the ___E:reunification of Germany U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_reunification)___ .

At the ___E:1999 Washington summit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_Washington_summit)___ , Hungary, Poland, and the Czech Republic officially joined, and NATO issued new guidelines for membership, with individualized " ___E:Membership Action Plans U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Membership_Action_Plan)___ ".

These plans governed the addition of new members: Bulgaria, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Romania, Slovakia, and Slovenia in 2004, Albania and Croatia in 2009, Montenegro in 2017, and North Macedonia in 2020.  Finland and Sweden are the newest members, joining in 2023 and 2024 respectively, spurred on by ___E:Russia's invasion of Ukraine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine)___ .

___E:Ukraine's relationship with NATO U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukraine%E2%80%93NATO_relations)___ began with the NATO–Ukraine Action Plan in 2002.  In 2005, Russian president ___E:Vladimir Putin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Putin)___ said that if Ukraine joined NATO, "we will respect their choice, because it is their sovereign right to decide their own defence policy, and this will not worsen relations between our countries".
However, since his ___E:2007 Munich speech U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_Munich_speech_of_Vladimir_Putin)___ , Putin has strongly opposed further enlargement.

In 2010, under President ___E:Viktor Yanukovych U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viktor_Yanukovych)___ , Ukraine re-affirmed its non-aligned status and renounced aspirations of joining NATO.  During the ___E:2014 Ukrainian Revolution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Ukrainian_Revolution)___ , Russia ___E:occupied Crimea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_occupation_of_Crimea)___ and supported ___E:armed separatists in eastern Ukraine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_separatist_forces_in_Ukraine)___ .

Because of this, in December 2014 Ukraine's parliament voted to end its non-aligned status,  and in 2019 it enshrined the goal of NATO membership in the ___E:Constitution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Ukraine)___ .

At the June ___E:2021 Brussels Summit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Brussels_summit)___ , NATO leaders affirmed that Ukraine would eventually join, and supported Ukraine's right to self-determination without interference.
In late 2021, there was another massive ___E:Russian military buildup U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prelude_to_the_Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine)___ on Ukraine's borders.

Russian president Putin warned that Ukraine joining NATO, and the deployment of ___E:missile defense systems U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_national_missile_defense)___ or long-range missiles in Ukraine, would ___E:cross a red line U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_line_(phrase))___ .
However, Ukraine was a long way from potential membership, and there were no such plans to deploy missiles.

The Russian Foreign Ministry drafted a treaty that would forbid Ukraine or any former Soviet state from ever joining NATO.  Secretary-General Stoltenberg replied that the decision is up to Ukraine and NATO members, adding "Russia has no veto...and Russia has no right to establish a ___E:sphere of influence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere_of_influence)___ to try to control their neighbors".
NATO offered to improve communications with Russia and discuss missile placements and military exercises, as long as Russia withdrew troops from Ukraine's borders.

Instead, ___E:Russia invaded Ukraine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine)___ in February 2022. Ukraine applied for NATO membership in September 2022 after Russia proclaimed it had ___E:annexed the country's southeast U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_annexation_of_Donetsk,_Kherson,_Luhansk_and_Zaporizhzhia_oblasts)___ .

Georgia was promised "future membership" during the 2008 summit in Bucharest,  but US president ___E:Barack Obama U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama)___ said in 2014 that the country was not "currently on a path" to membership.

Russian leaders have said that NATO enlargement went against informal understandings between Soviet leader ___E:Mikhail Gorbachev U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikhail_Gorbachev)___ and European and US negotiators that allowed for peaceful German reunification.

A June 2016 ___E:Levada Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levada_Center)___ poll found that 68 percent of Russians think that deploying NATO troops in the ___E:Baltic states U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltic_states)___ and Poland – former Eastern bloc countries bordering Russia – is a threat to Russia.

In contrast, 65 percent of Poles surveyed in a 2017 [needs update] Pew Research Center report identified Russia as a "major threat", with an average of 31 percent saying so across all NATO countries,  and 67 percent of Poles surveyed in 2018 [needs update] favour US forces being based in Poland.

Of non- ___E:CIS U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_Independent_States)___ Eastern European countries surveyed by Gallup in 2016, [needs update] all but ___E:Serbia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serbia)___ and ___E:Montenegro U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montenegro)___ were more likely than not to view NATO as a protective alliance rather than a threat.

A 2006 study in the journal Security Studies argued that NATO enlargement contributed to ___E:democratic consolidation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_consolidation)___ in Central and Eastern Europe.  ___E:China U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China)___ also opposes further expansion.

Member states pay for NATO's three common funds (the civil and military budgets and the security investment programme) based on a cost-sharing formula that includes per capita gross national income and other factors.
In 2023–2024, the United States and Germany were the biggest contributors to the NATO budget at 16.2% each.
Member states pay for and maintain their own troops and equipment.
They contribute to NATO operations and missions by committing troops and equipment on a voluntary basis.

Since 2006, the goal has been for each country to spend at least 2 percent of its gross domestic product on its own defence; in 2014, a NATO declaration said that countries not meeting the goal would "aim to move towards the 2 percent guideline within a decade".

In July 2022, NATO estimated that 11 members would meet the target in 2023.  On 14 February 2024, NATO Secretary General ___E:Jens Stoltenberg U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jens_Stoltenberg)___ said that 18 member states would meet the 2% target in 2024.  On 17 June 2024, prior to the ___E:2024 Washington summit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Washington_summit)___ , Stoltenberg updated that figure and announced that a record 23 of 32 NATO member states were meeting their defense spending targets of 2% of their country's GDP.   NATO added that defense spending for European member states and Canada was up 18% in the past year alone.

As of 2024, the following countries were not meeting the 2% contribution goal: Spain (1.28%), Luxembourg (1.29%), Slovenia (1.29%), Belgium (1.3%), Canada (1.37%), Italy (1.49%), Portugal (1.55%), and Croatia (1.81%).

The ___E:Partnership for Peace U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partnership_for_Peace)___ (PfP) programme was established in 1994 and is based on individual bilateral relations between each partner country and NATO: each country may choose the extent of its participation.
Members include all current and former members of the ___E:Commonwealth of Independent States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_Independent_States)___ .

The ___E:Euro-Atlantic Partnership Council U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euro-Atlantic_Partnership_Council)___ (EAPC) was first established on 29 May 1997, and is a forum for regular coordination, consultation and dialogue between all fifty participants.
The PfP programme is considered the operational wing of the Euro-Atlantic Partnership.
Other third countries have also been contacted for participation in some activities of the PfP framework, such as Afghanistan.

The European Union (EU) signed a comprehensive package of arrangements with NATO under the ___E:Berlin Plus agreement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Plus_agreement)___ on 16 December 2002. With this agreement, the EU was given the possibility of using NATO assets if it wanted to act independently in an international crisis, on the condition that NATO itself did not want to act – the so-called " ___E:right of first refusal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right_of_first_refusal)___ ".

For example, Article 42(7) of the 1982 ___E:Treaty of Lisbon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Lisbon)___ specifies that "If a Member State is the victim of armed aggression on its territory, the other Member States shall have towards it an obligation of aid and assistance by all the means in their power".

The treaty applies globally to specified territories, whereas NATO is restricted under its Article 6 to operations north of the ___E:Tropic of Cancer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropic_of_Cancer)___ .
It provides a "double framework" for the EU countries that are also linked with the PfP programme.
Additionally, NATO cooperates and discusses its activities with numerous other non-NATO members.

The ___E:Mediterranean Dialogue U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean_Dialogue)___ was established in 1994 to coordinate in a similar way with ___E:Israel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_relations_of_Israel)___ and countries in North Africa.

The ___E:Istanbul Cooperation Initiative U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Cooperation_Initiative)___ was announced in 2004 as a dialogue forum for the Middle East along the same lines as the Mediterranean Dialogue.
The four participants are also linked through the ___E:Gulf Cooperation Council U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_Cooperation_Council)___ .

In June 2018, Qatar expressed a wish to join NATO,  who ruled it out, saying that only additional European countries could join according to ___E:Article 10 of NATO's founding treaty U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Atlantic_Treaty#Article_10)___ .
Qatar and NATO had earlier signed a joint security agreement, in January 2018.
Political dialogue with Japan began in 1990, and since then, the Alliance has gradually increased its contact with countries that do not form part of any of these cooperation initiatives.
In 1998, NATO established a set of general guidelines that do not allow for a formal institutionalization of relations, but reflect the Allies' desire to increase cooperation.

Following extensive debate, the term "Contact Countries" was agreed by the Allies in 2000. By 2012, the Alliance had broadened this group, which meets to discuss issues such as counter-piracy and technology exchange, under the names " ___E:global partners U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO_global_partners)___ " or "partners across the globe".

Australia and New Zealand, both global partners,  are also members of the ___E:AUSCANNZUKUS U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AUSCANNZUKUS)___ strategic alliance, and similar regional or bilateral agreements between contact countries and NATO members also aid cooperation.

NATO Secretary General ___E:Jens Stoltenberg U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jens_Stoltenberg)___ stated that NATO needs to "address the ___E:rise of China U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Century)___ ", by closely cooperating with Australia, New Zealand, Japan and South Korea.

Colombia is NATO's latest partner and has access to the full range of cooperative activities offered; it is the first and only ___E:Latin American U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_American)___ country to cooperate with NATO.

NATO is an alliance of 32 sovereign states and their individual sovereignty is unaffected by participation in the alliance.
NATO has no parliaments, no laws, no enforcement, and no power to punish individual citizens.
As a consequence of this lack of sovereignty the power and authority of a NATO commander are limited.
NATO commanders cannot punish offences such as failure to obey a lawful order; dereliction of duty; or disrespect to a senior officer.

NATO commanders expect obedience but sometimes need to subordinate their desires or plans to the operators who are themselves subject to sovereign codes of conduct like the ___E:UCMJ U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UCMJ)___ .

A case in point was the clash between General ___E:Sir Mike Jackson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Jackson_(British_Army_officer))___ and General ___E:Wesley Clark U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wesley_Clark)___ over ___E:KFOR actions at Pristina Airport U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incident_at_Pristina_airport)___ .

NATO commanders can issue orders to their subordinate commanders in the form of operational plans (OPLANs), operational orders (OPORDERs), tactical direction, or fragmental orders (FRAGOs) and others.
The joint rules of engagement must be followed, and the ___E:Law of Armed Conflict U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_of_Armed_Conflict)___ must be obeyed at all times.

Operational resources "remain under national command but have been transferred temporarily to NATO. Although these national units, through the formal process of transfer of authority, have been placed under the operational command and control of a NATO commander, they never lose their national character." Senior national representatives, like ___E:CDS U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_of_the_Defence_Staff_(disambiguation))___ , "are designated as so-called red-cardholders".
Caveats are restrictions listed "nation by nation... that NATO Commanders... must take into account".
